title: Ang 370–411: Guru Arjan in Asa
hook: a great run of hymns, including your will is sweet on ang 394
tomorrow: why is a hymn about war so full of brides?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth guru: four wedding rounds and Asa hymns, sung in good company. Now the fifth Guru's long run of Asa hymns, and one short couplet in the middle of it.

Three days to the wedding. The tent company calls: the rental fell through. The forecast says rain. An aunt is on speaker, her voice climbing, and everyone turns to the bride to see whether she'll cry. She doesn't. She says, quietly, a line her grandmother says: tera keeaa meethaa laagai. What You do tastes sweet to me. It sounds like giving up. It isn't. It's a couplet from ang 394.
screen: `THREE DAYS OUT. NO TENT. RAIN.` → `EVERYONE WATCHES THE BRIDE.` → `WHAT YOU DO TASTES SWEET.`

segments.voice: Guru Arjan's Asa hymns run from ang 370 to 411, a long stretch, and in the middle sits this couplet, in paraphrase: what You do tastes sweet to me; Nanak asks for the treasure of the Name. Two lines. Notice what they don't say. They don't say the rain is good, or that the tent doesn't matter. They say the doing of the One tastes sweet, and then they ask for one thing. Not a better forecast. The Name. And sweet is a strange word for it. You'd expect accept, or put up with. Sweet is what you say about food you'd reach for again. Guru Arjan isn't describing gritted teeth. He's describing a taste that has changed. Tradition holds that he lived this line in his own last days, the hardest of his life, and Sikhs remember him that way, gently. It isn't a switch you flip on a bad Thursday. It's a taste you grow into, by asking for the Name over and over, the way the couplet does, until the plan falling apart and the sweetness can sit at the same table.
screen: `WHAT YOU DO TASTES SWEET.` · `ASK FOR ONE THING: THE NAME.` · `SWEET, NOT JUST PUT UP WITH.` · `A TASTE YOU GROW INTO.` · then, large: `SWEET WILL.`

segments.voice: Read ang 394 if you can, and find the couplet. Say it aloud once, slowly, in Gurmukhi or in English: what You do tastes sweet to me. Then sit with one thing this week that didn't go your way, and let the words rest beside it, without forcing anything.
Ang 370. The page where Guru Arjan's long run of Asa hymns begins; the sweet will couplet waits on ang 394.
Hold onto: sweet will, a taste you grow into, one ask for the Name at a time. Talk soon.

howItsDone: Guru Arjan's Asa hymns, headed Mahala 5, are read in order and sung as kirtan; the couplet on ang 394 is one Sikhs often turn to in hard times, remembering the fifth Guru.

fork.setup: your sister doesn't get into the school she wanted. through tears she says 'it's fine.' what fits ang 394?
options: let her be sad, and stay close; the sweetness comes slowly, with the Name.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape story (the hook is a scene mid-crisis three days before the wedding; the bride's line is the cliffhanger the teach explains). Answers yesterday's question: how can a plan falling apart taste sweet?

Ang 394 couplet (teraa keeaa meethaa laagai, har naam padaarath naanak maangai) paraphrased as 'what You do tastes sweet to me; Nanak asks for the treasure of the Name'. Confirm Ang. The popular phrase 'tera bhana meetha lage' is not used, to stay with the hymn's own words.
'Tradition holds that he lived this line in his own last days': hedged, with no details of the martyrdom given (one gentle line, suitable for children). Confirm the association is fairly put.
howItsDone says Sikhs 'often' turn to the couplet in hard times: Keeper to confirm or soften.
Guru Arjan's Sri Rag hymns (day 1457) used the hot gust and the shelter; today's angle (sweetness, a changed taste) doesn't repeat it.
